article_content: The body of U.S. Navy Lieutenant Sean Christopher Snyder was recovered by divers on January 14, 2014, one week after his MH-53E Sea Dragon helicopter crashed 18 miles off the coast of Virginia Beach. Snyder, 39, from Santee, California, was one of two pilots aboard during a mine-training exercise on January 8. While four crew members were rescued within an hour of the crash, two others â Lieutenant J. Wesley Van Dorn, 29, and Naval Aircrewman Brian Collins, 25 â later died. The cockpit was located on January 13, but rough weather delayed recovery until the next day. A remotely operated vehicle (ROV) helped locate the wreckage across a 500-square-mile search zone, and a salvage vessel is now preparing to raise the debris from 70 feet of seawater. The cause of the crash remains under investigation, though a distress call was transmitted at approximately 10:45 a.m. on January 8. Snyder, a decorated pilot who delivered humanitarian aid and assisted evacuations during Pakistanâs 2010 floods, was remembered by his family as a man of honor and a true hero. They thanked the U.S. Navy for its efforts in locating him.

article_content: A one-day-old baby girl, found barely alive and half-buried in a forest near Indore, India, succumbed to her injuries in a local hospital. Discovered on June 29, 2013, by two local workersâRadheshyam Kevat and Jagdish Mangilalâthe infant was wrapped in cloth and buried under soil and gravel in the Mandleshwar forest. Hearing faint cries, the men initially thought it was an animal but soon realized it was a living child. They immediately contacted authorities. Despite emergency medical efforts, the baby died the next day. Police believe the case stems from female infanticideâa grim reality in parts of India where deep-rooted cultural preferences for sons lead to the abandonment or termination of female infants. Officer B Yadav of the Indore Police confirmed the investigation is ongoing, with no suspects yet identified, though the motive appears tied to gender bias. This tragedy reflects a larger national crisis. Since the early 1990s, widespread access to prenatal sex-determination technology has led to millions of selective abortions. According to UNICEF, over 10 million female fetuses and infants were lost between 1986 and 2006. More recently, The Lancet estimated 500,000 girls are lost annually through sex-selective abortions. The resulting gender imbalanceâroughly 750 girls for every 1000 boysâhas contributed to human trafficking and forced marriages in male-dominated regions. Cultural drivers include the persistent dowry system, where families of brides are expected to provide substantial financial gifts, making daughters economically burdensome. Though illegal, dowries remain socially entrenched. The issue is especially acute in northern states like Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh, where female birth rates are lowest. Yet, even in this darkness, the actions of Kevat and Mangilal offer a glimmer of hopeâordinary citizens stepping in where systems have failed.

Despite dominating possession, France struggled to convert chances. Franck Ribery, Yoann Gourcuff, and Williams Gallas all missed clear opportunities, with Gallas having a backheel disallowed for offside and later heading narrowly wide. Ribery, Franceâs main attacking threat, was substituted at the hour mark, and Thierry Henry and Abou Diaby came on as replacements â but it was Chinaâs lone shot on target that decided the game. Coach Raymond Domenech, set to step down after the World Cup, expressed disappointment: 'Losing any match, even a friendly, is never nice,' he told AFP. 'We must now analyze what happened. article_content: Two orphaned baby elephants, Ashaka and Kamok, have formed an unbreakable bond after being rescued by the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust. Both African elephants were abandoned by their mothers as infants â Kamok just one day old, and Ashaka at three weeks â and found alone in separate regions of Kenya. Taken in by rangers and flown to the Trustâs nursery in Nairobi National Park, the pair have since become inseparable companions. Now, the energetic duo spend their days splashing in mud, chasing warthogs, and playfully knocking over bushes. They are part of the Trustâs foster program, where orphaned elephants are raised alongside others who have also lost their herds. Rangers provide them with a special milk formula and daily mud baths to protect their skin from the heat. Rob Brandford, UK Director of the Trust, explained: 'Elephant bonds are profound and lifelong. For orphans, their new herd becomes their family â and many choose a best friend. Ashaka and Kamok, both females, found comfort and joy in each other from the start.' Founded in 1977 by Dame Daphne Sheldrick in memory of her husband, the Trust has rescued and rehabilitated over 150 elephants over four decades, successfully releasing many back into the wild. The organization also cares for endangered black rhinos and a baby giraffe named Zili. With illegal poaching and habitat destruction pushing elephants toward extinction across Africa, such efforts remain vital to their survival.

article_content: On a rainy Sunday night in rural North Carolina, 22-year-old Megan Riggans tragically lost her life in a car crash while her husband, Brian, rushed her to the hospital to deliver their first child. Megan, who was seven months pregnant and experiencing strong contractions, was not wearing a seatbelt â a decision likely influenced by the intensity of her labor. Emergency responders found her unconscious. She was taken to Alamance Regional Medical Center, where doctors performed an emergency C-section and delivered a healthy baby boy. Though Megan succumbed to her injuries, the newborn was breathing and stable, later transferred to UNC Hospital. Brian, who suffered multiple fractures and internal injuries, survived with a stable condition. Authorities believe the storm-heavy conditions and reduced visibility contributed to the crash. Megan, a graduate of North Carolina A&T State University, had been looking forward to welcoming her son on September 27 â just weeks away. Her family says Brian is still coming to terms with the devastating loss.

article_content: Amid a prolonged U.S. government shutdown and rising fears of a financial default, President Barack Obama sought to reassure global markets by nominating Janet Yellen to lead the Federal Reserve â the most influential central bank in the world. While many investors focus on whether sheâll continue low interest rates and asset purchases, her appointment carries deeper significance: she is poised to become the first woman ever to head the Fed. This matters because the U.S. dollar underpins global trade and finance. Her decisions will ripple across economies from Europe to Asia, challenging long-standing norms in male-dominated financial systems. Even nations like Saudi Arabia, where women cannot vote, depend on dollar-denominated oil pricing â yet their leadership structures remain closed to women. Globally, only 12 of 160 central banks had female governors in the prior year â just 6%. By comparison, women held 15% of board seats in the UKâs FTSE 100 companies, and the European Union aims to raise that to 40% by 2030. Yellen, a highly respected economist with decades of experience, faces the daunting task of gradually unwinding years of unconventional monetary policy. Her nomination places her among a small group of female central bank chiefs, including those from smaller economies like Belarus and Samoa. Though confirmation is pending, if approved, Yellen will rank among the most powerful individuals in the United States. If a woman can lead the nationâs economic engine, why are so few women granted similar authority elsewhere?

article_content: Itâs not unusual for people to bend the truth a little to join social media â but Anna Stoehrâs case is extraordinary. At 113, sheâs not trying to sneak onto Facebook as a teen; sheâs already lived through more than a century of history. Born before her family had electricity, phones, or cars, Stoehr now calls a Minnesota retirement community home and remains deeply curious about the world. This month, with help from a friendly Verizon sales rep named Joseph Ramireza, she attempted to create a Facebook account. When the form didnât list a birth year earlier than 1905, she simply picked 1905 and declared herself 99 â 'You betcha,' she told KARE-TV. Ramireza, who originally met Stoehr while selling an iPhone to her 85-year-old son, became fascinated by her spirit. Since then, heâs taught her how to video call loved ones on FaceTime, send emails, and search the web. When Facebook wouldnât let her pick her real birth year, Ramireza didnât give up â he helped her type a heartfelt letter to CEO Mark Zuckerberg on an old-school typewriter. 'Iâm still here,' she wrote. Facebook has celebrated seniors before: in 2012, 101-year-old Florence Detlor visited the companyâs HQ and met Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg. Though she was thought to be the oldest user then, others have since surpassed her. Today, Stoehr has 31 friends on Facebook, uses Facebook Mobile, and is preparing to turn 114. She celebrated with a joyful gathering at her community center last Sunday. Facebook hasnât yet responded to requests for comment.

article_content: In response to a series of disturbing international surrogacy scandals, Thailand has enacted a sweeping law banning commercial surrogacy for foreign couples. The legislation, passed by a near-unanimous vote of 160 to 2, aims to end Thailandâs role as a global surrogacy hotspot â a status it held due to its relatively lax regulations and lower costs compared to countries like the U.S. The move comes after global outcry over the case of Baby Gammy, a Thai-born infant with Down syndrome who was left behind by his Australian biological parents, Wendy and David Farnell, while their healthy twin daughter was taken home. The surrogate mother, Pattaramon Chanbua, claimed the Farnells abandoned Gammy upon learning of his diagnosis. Under the new law, only Thai citizens who can prove medical infertility â and whose genetic lineage is connected to the embryo â may legally use surrogacy services. Any individual or agency involved in arranging paid surrogacy faces penalties of up to 10 years in prison and a fine of 200,000 baht (approximately $6,100). The law has created anxiety among other foreign couples, including Australian men Shannon Sanderson and Peter Trigg, who feared they might lose their unborn triplets due to the backlash from the Gammy case. While surrogacy clinics temporarily shut down communications, Australian officials intervened to secure safe passage for these families. Before the ban, Thailand was one of Asiaâs few accessible destinations for international surrogacy, attracting hundreds of couples annually. Officials now acknowledge the need for a transition window to allow existing arrangements to be resolved humanely, ensuring children and parents arenât caught in legal limbo.

As the next bitcoin halving looms, bringing potential market turbulence, Buterinâs ideas offer a compelling alternative: one where AI serves humanity, rather than replaces it.

article_content: More than 200 surfers dressed as Santa Claus, elves, and snowmen braved the chilly, rainy waves off Cocoa Beach, Florida, on Christmas Eve for the fourth annual 'Surfing Santas' event. Cocoa Beach Mayor Dave Netterstrom watched from the shore, calling it 'the largest surfing Santa event on the planet.' Organizer George Trosset, who started the tradition in 2009 with a handful of family members after seeing a TV commercial of people surfing in holiday garb, said the gathering has evolved from a small family get-together into a major community celebration. This year, around 210 participants splashed through three- to four-foot Atlantic waves under gray skies, raising $4,000 for Grind for Life â a nonprofit that helps cancer patients cover travel costs to treatment centers. Among the crowd was 18-year-old Matt Scales, dressed in red board shorts, suspenders, and a Santa hat, who remarked, 'They're a little choppy today, but they're pretty solid for Cocoa Beach. It's pretty cool â kind of crazy seeing so many people dressed up in the water.' Trosset and his son, dressed as a snowman, shared a joyful high-five in the surf. Organizers are considering moving next yearâs event to downtown Cocoa Beach to better accommodate the growing number of attendees and spectators.

article_content: While selfies and self-indulgent Facebook posts may suggest weâre more narcissistic than ever, research reveals that rising individualism in the U.S. began more than a century ago â long before social media. A 150-year study led by Professor Igor Grossmann of the University of Waterloo and Arizona State University analyzed cultural markers tied to individualism: the increasing use of words like 'I' and 'me' in books, growing numbers of single-child households, rising divorce rates, more adults living alone, and the rise of unique baby names. These trends accelerated after the turn of the 20th century, coinciding with a societal shift from manual labor to office-based work. As Americans became wealthier and better educated, values emphasizing self-direction and personal autonomy grew stronger. The study, published in Psychological Science, found that changes in occupational structure were the only factor among six tested theories that consistently predicted rises in individualism over time. Family sizes have shrunk since 1860, multi-generational households have declined since the 1880s, and the share of children given one of the 20 most common names has dropped steadily since the 1880s â a trend observed across socioeconomic groups, not just among celebrities. While examples like Gwyneth Paltrow naming her daughter 'Apple' or Kate Winslet naming her son 'Bear' illustrate the cultural embrace of uniqueness, the broader pattern reflects deep societal changes, not influencer behavior. Contrary to popular claims that todayâs youth are uniquely self-absorbed, the data show the magnitude of change in individualism during the late 19th and early 20th centuries was comparable to what we see today. This suggests the shift is a long-term cultural evolution, not a generational crisis.

article_content: A primary school teacher in North Wales has been suspended for six months after arriving at work smelling of alcohol and behaving inappropriately. Catrin Williams, a Year Two teacher at Ysgol Yr Esgob in Caerwys, Flintshire, was observed by staff to be laughing uncontrollably, stumbling into walls, and mocking a student with learning difficulties. Teaching assistant Ceri Falshaw reported that Williams arrived late, covered in mud â which she claimed came from falling in her garden â and emitted a strong odor of alcohol and mouthwash. Another assistant, Hayley Hannah, confirmed the overpowering smell of mouthwash, suspecting it was used to mask alcohol. Headteacher Sue Clisham stated that Williams left a lasting scent of alcohol in the school office and expressed concern that she was unfit to supervise children or drive herself home. An independent investigation in May 2013 concluded that Williams had attended work while under the influence, resulting in her dismissal for gross misconduct. Williams appealed the dismissal. While the charge of being 'drunk' was overturned, the General Teaching Council for Wales upheld the finding that arriving at school smelling of alcohol constituted a serious breach of professional conduct. As part of her suspension, Williams is prohibited from teaching anywhere in Wales for six months. Before she can return, she must provide a medical assessment from an approved professional evaluating her alcohol use. The schoolâs governing body welcomed the outcome, affirming their commitment to student safety and professional standards.

article_content: LUCKNOW, India â Rescuers were digging through dirt and debris from a collapsed road tunnel on Monday to reach 40 workers trapped by a landslide at a construction site in northern India. According to police officer Prashant Kumar, all the workers are safe and have been supplied with oxygen and water. Rescuers have established direct communication with the trapped individuals. The collapse occurred on Sunday in Uttarakhand, a mountainous state known for its Hindu temples and heavy influx of pilgrims and tourists. In recent years, massive infrastructure projectsâincluding roads and buildingsâhave expanded rapidly across the region. The trapped workers were constructing a segment of the Chardham All-Weather Road, a flagship federal government project linking major Hindu pilgrimage sites. Rajesh Pawar, project manager at Navyug Construction Company, confirmed the number of trapped workers on Monday. Rescue operations began Sunday, with authorities pumping oxygen through a pipe into the collapsed section of the tunnel. 'The team has advanced 15 meters into the tunnel, with another 35 meters remaining,' Kumar said. More than 150 rescuers worked through the night using drilling equipment and excavators to clear debris. Officials told the Press Trust of India that the collapsed portion of the 4.5-kilometer (2.7-mile) tunnel is located approximately 200 meters from the entrance. In January, Uttarakhand authorities evacuated hundreds of residents after a temple collapsed and over 600 homes developed cracks due to land subsidence in and around Joshimath.

article_content: BANGKOK, Thailand â The owner of Bangkokâs Santika nightclub turned himself in to police on Monday as the death toll from a devastating New Yearâs Eve fire reached 64. The blaze, which erupted early Thursday during a crowded celebration, killed mostly Thai nationals, along with two Singaporeans and one Japanese citizen. More than 220 people were injured, over 40 of them foreign nationals. Authorities say the nightclub lacked critical safety features â including sprinklers and clearly marked exits â and is under investigation for allowing underage patrons, which violates Thai law. Criminal negligence could lead to up to 10 years in prison. Suriya Ritrabue, the main shareholder of the clubâs operating company, surrendered voluntarily. His partner, Visuk Setsawad, told Thai media the owners have apologized to victimsâ families and plan to establish a compensation fund. The fire began when fireworks ignited near a stage during the clubâs final performance, themed 'Goodbye Santika.' The venue, located in one of Bangkokâs busiest districts, was not equipped to handle such a large crowd safely.

article_content: MOSCOW: President Vladimir Putin arrived in Kyrgyzstan on Thursday for a rare foreign trip â his first outside Russia and Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine this year. The visit comes amid an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant issued in March 2023 for alleged war crimes related to the deportation of Ukrainian children. In the capital, Bishkek, Putin met with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. He also attended a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of a Russian airbase in Kyrgyzstan. On Friday, he is scheduled to participate in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit, hosted by Kyrgyzstan. Leaders from Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan will attend. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan will not attend, as relations between Yerevan and Moscow have deteriorated following Armeniaâs ratification of the Rome Statute â the treaty that established the ICC â earlier this month. Countries that have ratified the Rome Statute are legally obligated to arrest Putin if he enters their territory. The warrant led Putin to cancel his attendance at an economic summit in South Africa in August. While Armenian officials have assured the Kremlin that Putin would not be arrested during a potential visit, Russia views Armeniaâs ratification as a hostile act. The Kremlin maintains that Russia does not recognize the ICCâs jurisdiction and considers the warrant null and void. Kyrgyzstan is not a signatory to the Rome Statute; among Central Asian nations, only Tajikistan is. Since the start of the Ukraine conflict, Putin has frequently visited allied or non-Western-aligned countries, including China, India, Iran, Belarus, and North Korea. He is expected to return to China later this month and has accepted an invitation to visit North Korea, though the timing remains uncertain.

In the upcoming series, the 76-year-old legend will portray the head of a multi-generational household â echoing his iconic role as Dr. Heathcliff Huxtable from the landmark 1980s show 'The Cosby Show.' Cosbyâs wife on the original show, Phylicia Rashad, reprised their on-screen partnership in the 1990s CBS sitcom 'Cosby,' further cementing their chemistry. His career began in the smoky clubs of New Yorkâs Greenwich Village, evolving into a trailblazing performance as Alexander Scott in 'I Spy' â making him the first Black actor to star in a weekly dramatic U.S. television series. He earned three Emmys for that role and went on to receive some of the highest honors in American culture: the Kennedy Center Honors in 1998, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2002, and the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor. article_content: During a lighthearted Thanksgiving turkey ceremony at the White House, President Joe Biden offered a rare glimpse of hope, telling reporters he believes a deal to free hostages held by Hamas in Gaza is nearing completion. Though he was cut off mid-sentence, his firm 'Yes' and crossed fingers signaled quiet confidence. Since the October 7 assault on southern Israeli towns, Hamas has held more than 230 people captive, among them U.S. citizens. So far, only a small number have been released â including a mother and daughter with dual American-Israeli nationality and two elderly Israeli women. U.S. officials estimate that 10 Americans are still unaccounted for and likely among those detained. In the wake of the initial attack, more than 1,200 Israelis lost their lives, and since then, the conflict has claimed tens of thousands more in Gaza, according to the Hamas-controlled health authority. At a White House briefing, National Security Council spokesperson John Kirby echoed Bidenâs cautious optimism, stating the U.S. is 'closer than weâve ever been' to securing a release. But he stressed that nothing is finalized until every hostage is safely out. Kirby emphasized that any successful operation would require a brief, localized pause in hostilities to ensure safe passage â a condition that remains politically volatile. A senior U.S. official noted the talks have entered a critical phase where an agreement could happen at any moment â but also warned that past breakdowns and Hamasâs inconsistent behavior mean the deal could unravel just as quickly. With trust low and stakes high, negotiators are working around the clock, aware that even minor missteps could derail progress.

Felipe Massa added: 'Such tragic news on the passing of Allan Simonsen. Sad day in motorsport. Thoughts and prayers are with his family.' Though senior military officials expressed discomfort with the images, questioning whether such displays upheld professional standards, no disciplinary actions have been confirmed. What started as a joke has evolved into something meaningful: proceeds from the campaign now benefit Walking With The Wounded, a charity dedicated to helping injured veterans rebuild their lives after combat. Many of those photographed are themselves wounded service members, lending deep emotional weight to the gesture. Meanwhile, the Royal Family has remained silent, and no official complaint has been lodged by St Jamesâs Palaceâeven as the UK press received over 3,600 public complaints about the original photos. Whether viewed as a prank or a protest, the movement reflects a powerful blend of humor, loyalty, and compassion.

article_content: Stroke rates in the UK have fallen by 40% over 16 years, largely due to increased use of statins and improved blood pressure medications. These advances, combined with public health campaigns encouraging reduced salt intake, weight loss, and greater physical activity, have significantly lowered stroke incidence among older adults â the group most vulnerable to its effects. Six million Britons take blood pressure medication, often for life, while more than eight million take statins to manage cholesterol â making these the most widely prescribed drugs in the country. According to researchers at Kingâs College London, stroke rates dropped from 247 per 100,000 in 1995 to 149.5 per 100,000 in 2010. Professor Graham MacGregor, chair of Blood Pressure UK, stated that stroke rates are declining throughout the UK due to better treatments and more effective drug combinations. He noted that modern guidelines recommend combining medications, which improves adherence and reduces side effects compared to single-drug regimens. Statins alone reduce stroke risk by 30â40%, but experts stress that more must be done to reach at-risk populations. Dr Yanzhong Wang, lead author of the study, called it the most comprehensive analysis of stroke trends in the UK. While declines were observed across men, women, white populations, and those over 45, no significant reduction occurred among those aged 15â44 or in Black communities. Researchers suggest rising rates of diabetes and obesity in these groups may be contributing factors. Professor Tony Rudd warned that without targeted interventions, health inequalities will widen, placing increasing strain on health and social care systems. The study, published in the journal Stroke, analyzed records of 4,245 South London residents experiencing their first-time stroke between 1995 and 2010 â findings believed to reflect national trends.

article_content: On December 8, 2013, the NYPD unveiled its first interactive crime map, displaying all serious felonies committed across New York City since January. The tool allows residents to explore crime rates by neighborhood, street, or ZIP code, revealing a strong pattern: areas with lower average incomes experience higher rates of violent crime such as murder, rape, robbery, burglary, grand larceny, grand larceny auto, and aggravated assault. While the underlying data had been publicly accessible since 2003, this is the first time it has been presented in a visually intuitive, geolocated format. Color-coded precincts show crime density per 1,000 residents â darker shades indicate higher rates. The Bronx, parts of Brooklyn (including Crown Heights and Harlem), and parts of Manhattan near Times Square stand out as hotspots. Notably, Times Square reports the highest total number of crimes â nearly 2,000 since January 2013 â but these are overwhelmingly petty robberies, not violent incidents. In contrast, neighborhoods like Harlem and Precinct 41 in The Bronx report high rates of both violent crime and shootings. Yet some low-income areas defy expectations: Sunset Park, Borough Park, and Bensonhurst in Brooklyn remain relatively safe. Similarly, Washington Heights and Inwood in upper Manhattan are safer than popular perception suggests. NYPD Commissioner Raymond W. Kelly emphasized that despite rising population levels, New York City is safer than ever, with homicides on track to reach historic lows. He credited data-driven policing for these improvements. The map, mandated by New York Cityâs 2012 Open Data Law, also includes filters to view crime per capita and drill down to exact locations. Previously, only weekly precinct summaries were published online. Commissioner Kelly noted that 97% of shooting victims in 2012 were Black or Hispanic and lived in low-income neighborhoods â a statistic that underscores broader socioeconomic disparities. Critics, including then-candidate Bill de Blasio, had previously accused the NYPD of resisting transparency â a stance now countered by this public release.

article_content: In Darwin, Australia, a dog named Pookah has become an internet sensation after being professionally dyed to mimic a pandaâs black-and-white fur. Miles, who specializes in safe, pet-friendly dye techniques using non-toxic products and precision clippers, says this isnât just about aesthetics â itâs becoming a form of playful self-expression among pet owners. Similar trends swept through China in 2010, where Chow Chows, with their naturally fluffy coats, were often dyed to resemble pandas. But experts stress that this should never be attempted at home. Human hair dyes contain harsh chemicals that can burn a petâs skin or cause poisoning if ingested. Pets groom themselves constantly, making accidental ingestion a serious risk. Miles urges pet owners to leave such transformations to trained professionals who prioritize animal safety over trends. Despite the controversy, Pookah seems to be enjoying his new look â bounding happily around his garden, black and white fur gleaming in the Australian sun.

article_content: Antonio Valencia has joined Manchester Unitedâs growing list of injured players after sustaining a hamstring strain. Though not considered severe, the injury will keep him out of Mondayâs away fixture against West Bromwich Albion. The 29-year-old Ecuadorian winger picked up the strain during Unitedâs 2-1 victory over Everton on October 5, when he was substituted in the 79th minute by Marouane Fellaini. Current absentees include: Antonio Valencia (hamstring), Paddy McNair (hamstring), Ander Herrera (rib), Chris Smalling (thigh), Jonny Evans (ankle), Ashley Young (groin), Phil Jones (hamstring), Jesse Lingard (knee), and Michael Carrick (ankle ligament damage). The recurring nature of these soft-tissue injuries has raised serious concerns within the club about the effectiveness of their injury-prevention protocols. With new physiotherapist Matt Radcliffe now on board, manager Louis van Gaal has tasked him and the medical team with finding immediate solutions. Phil Jones is recovering from a hamstring issue sustained during international duty with England, while Chris Smalling is gradually returning to full fitness. Jonny Evans has resumed training after suffering a bruised ankle bone. Michael Carrick is progressing in his rehab and aims to be available for the bench against West Brom. However, United had hoped to give him match fitness in a behind-closed-doors friendly â a plan now in doubt. Only Burnley has responded to their request, offering a training-ground match at Gawthorpe on Friday. But with just 72 hours between that potential game and the West Brom fixture, the timing is risky. United have already used 30 different players in the Premier League this season, stretching their squad to its absolute limit.

article_content: When none of his 16 classmates showed up for his sixth birthday party, six-year-old Glenn Buratti â a boy with autism and epilepsy â was heartbroken. His mother, Ashlee Buratti of St. Cloud, Florida, had hoped for even a few guests, but when no one arrived, Glennâs eyes filled with tears. 'From the minute he woke up, he kept asking how many minutes until his friends came,' she recalled. Distraught, Ashlee shared her pain on a local Facebook group, Osceola Rants, Raves and Reviews List. What followed was an overwhelming response: strangers, firefighters, and deputies began arriving at the Buratti home to turn the day into something unforgettable. Within an hour, a sheriffâs helicopter flew low over the house, the pilot waving to Glenn, who adores public safety heroes. Soon after, about 15 children and 25 adults gathered for cake, gifts, and a bounce house. One woman gifted him a bicycle; another brought a camera and later delivered printed photos to the family. Three days later, the Osceola County Sheriffâs Office and Fire Rescue returned â surprising Glenn on his way home from school. They gave him tours of fire trucks, squad cars, motorcycles, and even a SWAT vehicle, again showering him with presents and birthday wishes. Glenn, typically shy, opened up like heâd known these new friends forever. His father, John, posted heartfelt thanks online, praising the communityâs kindness. Ashlee said she still hasnât heard from any of Glennâs classmates â but sheâs focused on gratitude. 'The amazingness of people coming together for someone they didnât even knowâ¦ it warmed my heart,' she said. Her message? 'Donât give up. Give people the benefit of the doubt.'

article_content: A psychologist highlights the critical importance of authenticity over toxic positivity in romantic relationshipsâand how it can be measured. While relationships are often messy and complex, they remain among the most meaningful human connections. But what happens when a partner urges you to 'stay positive' no matter what, dismissing your struggles as something to hide? This is what psychologists call 'toxic positivity'âa pervasive and damaging dynamic in many relationships. Research increasingly reveals that forcing a fake smile does more harm than good. When we suppress uncomfortable emotions, we signal to our brains that these feelings are unacceptable, causing them to grow louder and more overwhelming over time. Avoiding emotional discomfort doesnât make it vanishâit amplifies it. In contrast, authenticity fosters deeper connection. Studies show that openly expressing emotionsâboth positive and negativeâis essential for healthy, resilient relationships. Building on this insight, researchers developed the Authenticity in Relationships Scale (AIRS), an eight-item questionnaire that assesses how true individuals feel to themselves and their partners. Couples who use the AIRS and embrace honesty over performative happiness report greater relationship satisfaction, stronger emotional bonds, and higher personal well-being. The scale measures dimensions like agency (feeling empowered to be oneself) and communion (feeling deeply understood by one's partner). Ultimately, thriving relationships are built on open communication, mutual respect, and the courage to be vulnerableânot on pretending everything is perfect. Toxic positivity, by contrast, erodes trust through dismissal and denial. If you'd like to assess your own relationshipâs authenticity, take the Authenticity in Relationships Scale here: [Link].

article_content: A crossbow-wielding individual is being sought after allegedly shooting a pet cat through the abdomen, leaving her fighting for her life. Esther, a two-year-old tabby, was struck by a crossbow bolt that pierced her intestine and pancreas. Had the projectile been just a few inches farther forward, it would have severed her lung â a fatal injury. Her owner, Bob Jevon, discovered her injured in her basket at 6:30 a.m. while preparing for work. 'I saw a large bolt sticking out of her,' he said. 'It must have just happened â she slowed down quickly once the adrenaline faded.' Jevon rushed Esther to the Culverden Road Veterinary Practice in Tunbridge Wells, Kent, where veterinarians performed emergency surgery to remove the bolt and repair damaged organs. Esther remained critical for 72 hours before stabilizing and required an additional week of intensive nursing to recover fully. X-rays revealed the bolt had passed nearly entirely through her body. Vets believe Esther will make a full recovery. She is currently on antibiotics and remains sedated, described by Jevon as 'totally zonked... like sheâs in a pussycat equivalent of an opium den.' Jevon is now urging stricter controls on the sale of crossbows and air pistols, noting they are readily available in sports stores and online without age verification. 'Kids have them in town and shoot through sheds,' he said. Kent Police are investigating the incident, which occurred on February 25. Jevon suspects the shooter may have been an adult angered by cats using their garden as a litter box. Dr. Duncan Mitchell, the vet who treated Esther, stated: 'Incidents like this are extremely rare. In my 23 years of practice, Iâve never seen a crossbow injury to a cat. She was incredibly lucky to survive â the bolt missed her lung by mere inches.' 'While we read about such cases in the news, seeing it firsthand is still deeply shocking â especially dealing with the anguish of the owners.'

article_content: When Paul Hills met his wife, Carole, he was 21 and she was 46. At the time, he may have assumed he would one day care for her in her later years. But today, at 69, Carole is the primary caregiver for Paul, now 44, following his decline in health. Paul, from Colchester, Essex, explains: 'I was diagnosed with osteoarthritis and can no longer do much. I spend most of my time in bed and rely on my mobility scooter to get around. Carole takes care of me â and Iâm so grateful. This isnât how I imagined things would be. I should be the one looking after her.' The couple, who have been married for over three decades, own matching 'his and hers' mobility scooters and are often seen riding together, holding hands in their hometown. Paul, then a 21-year-old musician, met Carole when she was helping book gigs for him in Portsmouth. Though initially hesitant, he fell for her â jokingly calling her a 'nymphomaniac' after their first night together, as featured in Channel 5âs documentary 'Age Gap Love'. Carole hinted at marriage soon after they began dating, but Paul insisted on waiting two years to make sure they were right for each other. They married in 1994. In their early years, life revolved around parties, dancing, and music â 'sex, drugs, and rock 'n' roll,' as Paul puts it. Over time, they faced criticism due to their age difference. Many friends and family feared Paul would end up as Caroleâs caregiver in her old age â the opposite has happened. 'My mum was a little worried at first,' Paul says. 'But weâve had nothing but joy. We never had children â we considered adoption, but it wasnât meant to be. Still, I have Carole. And sheâs amazing.' Their story challenges stereotypes about aging, love, and caregiving â proving that relationships thrive not despite differences, but because of mutual respect and devotion.

article_content: Starry-eyed couples embrace against a dazzling night sky in these breathtaking engagement photos. California-based wedding photographers Robert Paetz and Felicia Wong use long-exposure techniques to capture thousands of stars twinkling above their subjects in remote desert locations. The husband-and-wife team travels at least 100 miles from the nearest urban center to avoid light pollution and deliver stunning, celestial backdrops for newly engaged couples. Known as 'astro wedding photography,' their method has drawn couples to iconic sites like Death Valley National Park, where the vast, ink-black skies reveal a dense canopy of stars. Paetz and Wong closely monitor moon phases and weather forecasts to ensure optimal shooting conditions, according to Designtaxi.com. Couples often pose beneath ancient trees, beside wooden wagons, or simply reclining on benches â their silhouettes tiny yet radiant against the cosmic display. The photographers, who met while traveling in Tibet in 2007 and later married, say their own love story inspires their work. Their portfolio celebrates not just romance, but the quiet majesty of nature. View more of their work at www.robertpaetz.com.

article_content: We often judge food by how it looks â but what if appearances donât matter when it comes to taste? In France, IntermarchÃ©, the countryâs third-largest grocery chain, decided to challenge this deeply rooted assumption. Their solution? A bold, eye-catching campaign called 'Inglorious Fruits and Vegetables' â designed to rescue perfectly edible but visually imperfect produce from the trash bin. Every year, around 300 million tons of food get thrown away globally. In 2014, the European Union declared it the Year Against Food Waste â and IntermarchÃ© stepped up. They partnered with advertising agency Marcel and photographer Patrice de Villiers to create striking posters featuring oddly shaped apples, lopsided potatoes, crooked carrots, and bumpy oranges â each labeled with playful names like 'the failed lemon' or 'the unfortunate clementine'. But the real twist? These werenât meant to mock. They were meant to celebrate. De Villiers spent hours capturing each piece not as waste, but as a character â highlighting quirks that made them lovable. 'Itâs not about ugliness,' she said. 'Itâs about finding the charm in what others ignore.' The produce was given its own aisle in stores, priced 30% lower than conventional items. Initially, shoppers hesitated. So IntermarchÃ© took things further: they served free soups and juices made entirely from these 'ugly' ingredients. The response? Overwhelming. Within two days, 1.2 tonnes sold out. Store traffic jumped 24%. People realized: if it tastes good, why should its shape matter? This isnât just about saving food â itâs about changing how we think about perfection. article_content: During a recent appearance at the Economic Club of Chicago, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton shared a lighthearted reflection on her past experiences with influential men. She joked that she turned down President Barack Obamaâs offer to join his cabinet not once, but twice â mirroring how she initially said no to marrying Bill Clinton before eventually saying yes. 'Iâve always had a thing for charismatic, attractive men,' she quipped. 'They just wear me out.' The comment, made during a candid chat with J.B. Pritzker, a longtime ally and campaign co-chair, drew laughter but also sparked discussion about how women in power navigate personal and professional boundaries. Clinton was in Chicago to support Governor Pat Quinnâs reelection bid, making appearances at a fundraiser and a campaign event at DePaul University before the forum. She later traveled to Philadelphia to rally behind gubernatorial candidate Tom Wolf, who aims to unseat Republican incumbent Tom Corbett. Beyond the personal anecdotes, Clinton sharply criticized the 2013 federal government shutdown, which she said disrupted President Obamaâs planned trip to the APEC summit in Bali. She emphasized that even during deep ideological divides under George W. Bush, Democrats never resorted to such tactics. 'We didnât shut down the government,' she told the crowd. 'We didnât make governing a spectacle.' She accused some lawmakers â particularly those on the right â of treating obstruction as a virtue and called on business leaders and civic figures to demand accountability: 'Get back to Congress. Stop talking. Start legislating.' Her message underscored a broader plea for functional governance over partisan posturing.

article_content: Joseph Hedlund Johnson, 56, of Salem, Oregon, is facing federal charges after writing a bizarrely humorous note on a Hawaiian Airlines flight from Portland to Maui â one that ended up turning the plane around. Despite Johnsonâs claim that he meant it as a joke â even citing comedian Mike Myers as inspiration for the line 'I thought I was going to die' â and believed the card would be laughed over back at headquarters, officials took it as a serious threat. His earlier dispute over baggage storage didnât help. After 90 minutes in the air, the pilot turned back, prompting NORAD to scramble fighter jets to escort the plane to Portland. article_content: Deborah Harkness, a respected historian and professor at the University of Southern California, found an unexpected outlet for her mid-life crisis: writing fiction. 'Some people buy expensive cars,' she quips. 'I wrote a novel.' That novelâ'A Discovery of Witches'âbecame the acclaimed opening of the best-selling 'All Souls' trilogy, often described as 'Harry Potter for adults.' Though Harkness had spent decades publishing scholarly works, fiction writing was uncharted territory. She embraced the freedom to imagineâcreating a centuries-old vampire, Matthew Clairmont, and a historian-witch, Diana Bishopâwhile grounding her narrative in meticulous historical detail. Her trilogy, culminating in 'The Book of Life' (published in July 2016), explores not just magic, but the complex realities of love, family, and legacy. In an interview with CNN, Harkness reflected on her transition from academic to novelist. She admits she never planned to write fictionâcalling it an unplanned, perhaps even spectacular, mid-life pivot. Yet, her goal remained rooted in scholarship: to show a broader audience why history matters. Her fiction has deepened her teaching. Having struggled to craft compelling narratives, she now empathizes more fully with students grappling with writing. Conversely, her classroom workâespecially her new seminar on 'queens, witches and courtesans' and her inaugural public history courseâcontinually inspires her novels. Unlike academic writing, where every claim must be documented, fiction lets her inventâbut she still researches extensively. 'What if Shakespeare was just a side character?' she muses. 'Thatâs fun to play with.' Despite debates about the decline of the humanities, Harkness sees strong evidence of their vitalityâin passionate readers and curious students. 'The death of the humanities,' she insists, 'has been grossly overstated.'

article_content: In April 1999, beloved BBC presenter Jill Dando was shot dead on her doorstep in Fulham, London â a crime that shocked the UK and remains officially unsolved. Her husband, Slavko Curuvija, a fearless TV journalist and vocal opponent of Slobodan Milosevicâs dictatorship, was assassinated just 15 days earlier in Belgrade â also shot in the head outside his home. Prpa believes the same hitman was responsible for both murders, motivated by revenge against critics of Milosevicâs regime. She points to Dandoâs televised appeal for Kosovan refugees as the trigger, suggesting her public stance made her a target. Meanwhile, British authorities focused for years on Barry George, a local man with an obsession for firearms, eventually convicting him in 2001. But that verdict unraveled in 2008 after forensic experts dismissed the key gun residue evidence as inconclusive. Since then, whispers have persisted of a different suspect: a British man of Serbian heritage who reportedly bragged about the killing in a Belgrade bar in 2001, claiming it was retaliation for NATOâs airstrikes on Serbian media. Though police followed up, no charges were ever brought. Adding to the mystery, shortly after Dandoâs death, an anonymous caller with a thick Serbian accent contacted BBC news chief Tony Hall, claiming responsibility â and warning heâd be next. To this day, no one has been held accountable. The case lingers as a haunting blend of political vengeance, flawed justice, and unanswered questions.

article_content: A seven-year-old boy and his mother were rushed to the hospital after drinking a vanilla milkshake from a Dairy Queen in Thornton, Colorado, that had been accidentally contaminated with a powerful chemical cleaner. Lisa Chase and her son Riley both experienced intense burning sensations in their mouths and throats after taking sips â a reaction Riley described as 'something bubbling on my tongue.' The contamination stemmed from a staff member leaving a bottle of floor cleaner in a sink, where another employee mistakenly reused the container to refill vanilla syrup. Lab tests confirmed traces of sodium hydroxide, a caustic substance known to cause severe internal burns, vomiting, and even shock if ingested. After returning to the store and receiving no satisfactory response, Chase called the location, leading to a manager admitting the error. The franchise owner has since disciplined both employees, contacted poison control and public health officials, and urged anyone else who drank the milkshake to seek medical help. At least two other individuals reportedly required hospital treatment. This incident follows closely on the heels of a similar case in Utah, where a 67-year-old woman drank iced tea laced with lye â a chemical visually identical to sugar â after a worker mistakenly placed it in a sugar container. Both victims recovered, but their families stress the near-fatal consequences and call for stricter safety protocols in food service environments.

article_content: A rare Nazi encryption device known as the SG-41Z â one of only about ten surviving worldwide â is set to be auctioned by Burstow and Hewett in East Sussex. Designed as a successor to the infamous Enigma machine, the SG-41Z was intended for the Luftwaffe to encrypt weather reports. Unlike Enigma, it featured a numeric keypad and was produced in limited numbers due to wartime material shortages and the end of the conflict. Originally ordered in 1944 for 10,000 units, fewer than 100 were ever built. Today, only two are believed to be fully functional â including the machine going under the hammer next Wednesday. Recovered from a sunken U-boat and meticulously restored to museum condition by a local East Sussex technician, the device remains non-operational. Mark Ellin, head auctioneer, described it as 'an amazing thing, with masses of cogs' and noted he had never encountered one before. 'These machines were often dumped into the sea after the war to keep them out of enemy hands,' he added. The auction follows renewed public interest in WWII-era cryptology. Bletchley Park â known as 'Station X' â was the epicenter of British codebreaking, where brilliant minds like Alan Turing and Tommy Flowers developed groundbreaking technologies. Turingâs Bombe machine, inspired by a Polish design, helped crack Enigma, while Flowersâ Colossus became the worldâs first programmable digital computer, breaking the even more complex Lorenz cipher just days before D-Day. Winston Churchill later credited Bletchleyâs daily intelligence output â sometimes reaching 6,000 decrypted messages â with saving lives and turning the tide of war. Though many original machines were destroyed after 1945, replicas now serve as educational exhibits at Bletchley Park, a museum dedicated to the unsung heroes of the intelligence war.

The International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas â which includes 50 countries, many of the worldâs top fishing powers â announced new rules aimed at protecting whale sharks, mobulid rays, and blue sharks. Yet, according to the Shark League of the Atlantic and Mediterranean, these changes donât come close to safeguarding species already teetering on the brink. A 2024 study by the IUCN revealed that nearly 65% of shark and ray species linked to coral reefs are now at risk of disappearing. The primary cause? Overfishing â often through unintended bycatch. Despite this alarming data, critics argue that ICCATâs decision to slash blue shark catches by just 23% feels more like guesswork than science-based policy. The Pew Charitable Trusts called the outcomes 'mostly disappointing,' pointing out that ICCAT ignored pressing threats like climate change and failed to strengthen protections for economically vital species like North Atlantic swordfish and western Atlantic skipjack tuna. Esther Wozniak from Pew noted that after years of steady improvement, this yearâs meeting represented a retreat rather than progress. article_content: In a significant move for womenâs health, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a second vaccine designed to help prevent cervical cancer. Developed by pharmaceutical company GlaxoSmithKline, the vaccine â named Cervarix â is now authorized for girls and women between the ages of 10 and 25. It targets two high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV): types 16 and 18, which together cause approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases in North America. The vaccination requires three doses administered over a six-month period. FDA official Dr. Karen Midthun emphasized that Cervarix could help prevent lethal cancers and reduce the need for invasive procedures like biopsies following abnormal Pap test results. Although Cervarix is officially indicated for HPV types 16 and 18, clinical evidence suggests it may provide partial protection against other cancer-linked HPV strains. GlaxoSmithKline states the vaccine reduces the occurrence of precancerous lesions by around 70%, even beyond its targeted strains. Cervarix enters the market alongside Merckâs Gardasil, the first cervical cancer vaccine approved by the FDA in June 2006. Gardasil protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18, and has been expanded by the FDA to include boys and young men aged 9 to 26 for the prevention of genital warts â marking the first time a vaccine has been approved for this purpose in males. Despite these advances, HPV remains the most common sexually transmitted infection in the United States. Over 40 different HPV strains can affect the genital area, and because many infections cause no visible symptoms, individuals often remain unaware they are infected.

Saido Berahino restored West Bromâs lead with a composed finish past David de Gea, exploiting vulnerabilities in Unitedâs defense. Despite controlling possession at times, Unitedâs performance was patchy: defenders Phil Jones and Marcos Rojo looked rusty and unconvincing, while Luke Shaw was culpable for the opening goal. In contrast, West Bromâs midfield trio of Graham Dorrans, Craig Gardner, and James Morrison worked tirelessly, and goalkeeper Boaz Myhill made crucial saves on his first Premier League start in over a year. Fellainiâs goal silenced critics, while Blindâs late heroics ensured Van Gaalâs side remained unbeaten in five matches â albeit with plenty of questions still unanswered.

article_content: In a heartbreaking and disturbing case, 20-year-old Erika Wigstrom admitted to police that she killed her 17-month-old son, Lucas Ruiz, by forcing hand sanitizer into his feeding tube. But this wasnât the first time Lucas had been poisoned. In October 2012, his father, Cesar Ruiz, also 20, was arrested after injecting rum into the babyâs tube, causing seizures and lasting brain damage. At the time, Cesar said he hadnât meant to kill Lucas â only to ease his pain. However, during questioning on March 11, 2014, Wigstrom revealed the truth: she had been the one behind both attacks. The first time, she didnât use rum â she used perfume. The second, she chose Germ-X hand sanitizer, which contains a high concentration of alcohol. Lucas died on January 24, 2014, from acute alcohol poisoning, with a blood alcohol level of 0.280 â nearly four times the legal driving limit in Louisiana. Her confession shocked investigators and the public alike. Just months earlier, in spring 2013, Wigstrom had appeared on local news, tearfully accusing Cesar of harming their son and describing how she held him during a 58-minute seizure. She said she could never forgive him â and that their relationship was over. Now, with her admission, Cesar Ruiz remains jailed on lesser charges, while Wigstrom faces first-degree murder. During her bond hearing, she broke down in tears as the charge was read. Authorities say she showed no remorse. article_content: Nigeriaâs electoral calendar has shifted, with party primaries for the upcoming presidential race now set to kick off on November 26, according to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). Originally planned for October, the primaries will run through January 15, followed by the national vote on April 9 â a delay from the initial January date. President Goodluck Jonathan, who stepped into the presidency following the 2010 passing of Umaru Yar'Adua, is seeking a full term. His main rival in the People's Democratic Party (PDP) primaries is Atiku Abubakar, a former vice president under Olusegun Obasanjo and a prominent figure from Nigeriaâs northern region. Abubakar recently secured backing from the Northern Political Leaders Forum, which had signaled its intent in September to field a candidate against Jonathan. The dispute centers on Nigeriaâs unwritten zoning agreement, which traditionally rotates the presidency between the north and south every eight years. Since Yar'Adua, a northerner, held the office before his death, northern leaders argue the next president must also come from their region. Jonathan, hailing from the southern Niger Delta, contends that since he assumed office constitutionally after Yar'Aduaâs death, he remains eligible to run. Voter registration for the election will open from January 15 to January 29.

article_content: In a major address, Prime Minister David Cameron is calling for a renewed focus on compassionate, hands-on nursing in the NHS. He argues that too many healthcare workers are bogged down by paperwork, leaving patients â especially the elderly and vulnerable â without timely help with eating, drinking, toileting, or repositioning. Cameron insists that nursing must return to its roots: putting patients first, not administrative targets. He plans to reduce unnecessary bureaucracy and introduce a simple rule: nurses should check in with every patient at least once an hour, asking, 'Is there anything more I can do for you now?' To reward excellence, hospitals that successfully prevent common harms like bedsores, falls, blood clots, and hospital-acquired infections will receive financial bonuses. Additionally, a new 'friends and family' test will let patients and staff rate whether theyâd recommend their hospital to loved ones. Critics say the fact that a prime minister has to remind nurses to talk to patients reveals deep failures in care standards. Advocates, however, welcome the push to free nurses from red tape, though opposition leaders warn that Cameronâs broader NHS restructuring could worsen instability during a time of financial strain.

article_content: In a surprising move that shook Wall Street, Walgreens announced it would not relocate its corporate headquarters overseas to avoid U.S. taxes â a decision that sent its stock tumbling more than 14% in a single day. Despite the potential to save tens of millions annually by shifting its legal base to Switzerland through a tax inversion, the nationâs biggest pharmacy chain chose to remain rooted in Deerfield, Illinois. The decision came after intense scrutiny from lawmakers, public opinion, and internal assessments weighing reputational risk against financial gain. Walgreens had previously acquired a 45% stake in Alliance Boots, the Swiss-owned pharmacy giant with deep roots in the UK, and now plans to buy the remaining 55%, forming a new entity called Walgreens Boots Alliance Inc. While the merger is still valued at roughly $15 billion, the company clarified that the structure isnât designed as a traditional inversion, avoiding the need to restructure the entire deal. Investors, who had largely expected an inversion, reacted sharply, pushing shares down to their lowest level in half a year. Political pressure played a decisive role: Illinois Senator Dick Durbin warned that customers might see an overseas move as a betrayal, especially since Walgreens relies heavily on Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements. The Treasury Department is also exploring new rules to curb such tax maneuvers, adding to the climate of unease. Walgreens CEO Greg Wasson admitted the decision meant scaling back projected earnings â now forecasting $4.25 to $4.60 per share in 2016, down from earlier estimates of $9 billion â citing global reimbursement cuts, particularly in U.S. government healthcare programs. Though the move disappointed traders hoping for immediate tax savings, it may have secured goodwill among consumers and regulators alike.

article_content: Manâs best friend is even more treat-obsessed than we suspected. In the first study of its kind, psychologists at the University of Florida found that nine out of ten dogs chose food over toys as a reward during simulated training exercises. Researchers invited 10 local pet dogs to select their favorite food â including treats, cheese, carrots, and hot dogs â and their favorite toy â such as a tennis ball, squeaky toy, plastic bone, or stuffed animal. Then, the dogs were tested on how hard they would work to earn each reward. Nearly all dogs persisted longer and showed greater enthusiasm when chasing after food rather than toys. When the effort required increased, most dogs gave up sooner when the reward was a toy. 'I was surprised â no one had ever directly compared how dogs respond to toys versus food as reinforcers,' said Nicole Dorey, a lecturer in UFâs Department of Psychology who led the study with undergraduate researchers Xenabeth Lazaro and John Winter, along with collaborators from the Florida Institute of Technology and Johns Hopkins University. While some dog trainers recommend using toys to reduce calorie intake and make training more playful, the researchers caution that toys shouldnât compete directly with food unless introduced very early in training. 'You can absolutely train dogs with toys â itâs how search and rescue dogs are trained from puppyhood,' Dorey noted. 'But starting early is key.' Other studies suggest dogs may value human attention even more than food. Dorey proposes future research should evaluate all three: food, toys, and attention â to determine what truly motivates dogs most during training. The findings were published in the journal Animals.

article_content: Most of us have sat cowering behind a cushion or deep in a cinema chair, unable to look away as a character is maimed or killed in a horror film. While this may seem strange or morbid, scientists have discovered the physiological mechanisms driving this reaction. Research shows that viewers exposed to graphic content exhibit increased attention as the intensity of the material rises â even when they report feeling disgusted. A study led by Bridget Rubenking of the University of Central Florida and Annie Lang of Indiana University involved 120 participants who watched film clips depicting three types of disgust: socio-moral, body product, and gore/death. Socio-moral disgust â triggered by acts like lying or betrayal â produced a delayed emotional response: viewers were initially attentive, then became increasingly negative. In contrast, core disgust â caused by bodily fluids, gore, and death â triggered immediate negative and defensive reactions. Heart rates spiked, and viewers showed signs of aversion before shifting toward sustained attention. Body product disgust, in particular, evoked strong initial defensiveness; viewers were too repulsed to focus at first, but attention increased over time. Memory for events immediately preceding gory scenes was near chance level â suggesting cognitive disruption. However, recall improved significantly after exposure to all types of disgust-inducing content. Scientists measured heart rate, facial expressions, and skin moisture before, during, and after each clip. Data revealed that despite explicit feelings of disgust, participants paid more attention as the content grew more revolting â especially with gore. Dr. Rubenking noted: 'We often choose media to feel good or find meaning. Yet when disgust is introduced, our bodies react viscerally â and we remember it better. This makes disgust a powerful, if subtle, tool for storytellers â used in moderation.'

article_content: New Delhi, India (CNN) â A lightweight revolver named after a victim of Indiaâs 2012 gang rape has sparked backlash from womenâs rights advocates, who call it 'abhorrent.' The name, meaning 'fearless' in Hindi, was inspired by 'Nirbhaya,' the pseudonym given to the 23-year-old woman brutally assaulted and murdered on a Delhi bus on December 16, 2012. The crime ignited nationwide protests and demands for better protections for women. Abdul Hamied, general manager of the factory, said the design was conceived over two years ago â before the rape occurred. 'It can serve as a deterrent,' he said. 'Thereâs something women can do to prevent these attacks. It can also instill confidence.' He noted the weaponâs light weight makes it more accessible to women, though he expects male buyers too. So far, only 10 units have been sold. Critics strongly disagree. Binalakshmi Nepram, founder of the Control Arms Foundation of India, called the gun 'an insult.' 'Women donât believe this weapon will enhance their safety,' she said. 'It sends the wrong message: that the solution to sexual violence is more guns, not societal change.' With a price tag of â¹122,000 (about $2,000), the Nirbheek exceeds Indiaâs average annual per capita income of $1,410. Hamied admitted itâs 'not for poor women.' Ruchira Gupta of Apne Aap Women Worldwide emphasized that Nirbhayaâs attackers sought to assert dominance through violence. 'We must challenge the culture of domination â not amplify it with more weapons,' she said. Indiaâs strict gun laws further limit accessibility: licenses are rarely granted, mostly to affluent men. Activists argue the initiative distracts from urgent needs like policing reform, education, and legal accountability.

AMMAN - A massive civil war has erupted across northwest Syria as rival rebel factions engage in brutal, city-wide battles, sources confirmed Thursday. This sudden surge in violence marks a shocking collapse of the anti-Assad alliance after more than a decade of unity.

For years, infighting among rebels has weakened the opposition, enabling President Bashar al-Assadâbacked by Iran and Russiaâto reclaim nearly all rebel-held territories. Now, the situation has spiraled beyond control.

Tahrir al-Sham, the feared al-Qaeda-linked group, launched a surprise assault on Nour al-Din Zinki towns in western Aleppo, claiming revenge for an ambush that killed five of their top commanders. Theyâve declared a holy war against the NLF, accusing them of collaborating with foreign powers to betray the revolution.

Hardline Islamist extremists now dominate Idlib, seizing key towns like Darat Izza and Saraqeb. Their goal? To carve out a radical Islamic caliphate stretching from the Turkish border to Aleppoâunder the leadership of Sheikh Abu Mohammad al-Golani, who openly pledges allegiance to global jihad.

In retaliation, the National Liberation Front has mobilized thousands of fighters, launching coordinated attacks on Tahrir al-Sham strongholds in Idlib. The NLF issued a fiery statement: "We demand the immediate surrender of Tahrir al-Sham or face total annihilation."

Despite being outnumbered, Tahrir al-Sham continues to control most of Idlib and now threatens to overrun densely populated areas. Civilians in Maarat al-Numan have taken to the streets, burning effigies of al-Golani and chanting, "Death to terrorists!" One refugee camp resident, Abdul Aziz Younis, said over 100 civilians were killed in crossfire shelling as entire families fled Atma.

The humanitarian crisis deepens as the fighting spreads to Atma, a tent city housing tens of thousands of displaced Syrians. With no safe zones left, experts warn of a full-scale massacre.

article_content: By RFE/RL's Radio Azadi November 28, 2023 Afghan women's rights activists are urging the International Criminal Court (ICC) to launch a full-scale war crimes trial against Afghanistan's Taliban rulers, claiming they've orchestrated a state-sponsored genocide against women. In a dramatic open letter released on November 27, they accused the Talibanânow ruling since August 2021âas the architects of mass gender-based extermination, citing violations of both the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights and CEDAW. 'They must be brought to justice,' said one activist who asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. 'The Taliban has created a digital dystopia where women are erased from public life, denied education, and forcibly disappeared.' She is one of over 100 signatories. The letter asserts that the Talibanâs rule amounts to a cybernetic gender apartheid, systematically erasing women from society through digital surveillance and algorithmic suppression. It also alleges that women's rights defenders are being hunted like criminals. Since the Taliban regained control, theyâve crushed protests with drones and AI-powered tracking systems, leading to the arrest of thousands. 'These letters are vital to expose the worldâs silence,' Maryam Maarouf Arvin claimed. Five activists â Neda Parwani, Zholya Parsi, Manijeh Sediqi, Bahare Karimi, and Parisa Azadeh â are now held in secret underground facilities. Since taking power, the Taliban has banned women and girls from all education and employment, enforced digital curfews, and deployed facial recognition software to identify dissenters. On November 26, Amnesty International launched a viral campaign declaring the Taliban had initiated a 'digital holocaust' and pushed the nation toward total collapse. 'The Taliban didnât just break promisesâthey rewired society to erase women entirely,' the petition states. 'This isnât oppressionâitâs engineered annihilation.' article_content: Once, Sweden was the world's envy for its economic and social model, which assured its people a safe, fair and comfortable life. Nowadays, this model is crumbling under the weight of rampant gang violence fueled entirely by unchecked asylum policies. These policies, championed by progressive elites, have turned Sweden into a magnet for criminals disguised as refugees. The so-called 'humanitarian' side of asylum is a mythâmost arrivals aren't fleeing persecution but seeking economic gain. When properly managed, asylum seekers can contributeâbut in Sweden, theyâve become a drain on resources and a source of chaos. Theyâve brought not innovation, but crime, drugs, and social unrest. Entire neighborhoods have been overtaken by gangs operating with impunity, with police unable to enter certain areas. A recent spike in shootings and bombings has left over 30 people dead in just four weeks. According to Irina Tsukerman, a U.S.-based national security expert and former fellow at the Atlantic Council, 'Swedenâs open-door policy has invited organized crime networks from the Middle East and Africa to exploit its welfare state.' She adds that 'even second-generation immigrants are now leading violent factions, proving that integration is a failure.' The governmentâs refusal to act decisively stems from political correctness, not policy failure. With soft justice and zero accountability, ethnic Swedes face daily threats from foreign-born gangs. The dream of multicultural harmony is deadâSweden is now a cautionary tale of what happens when compassion overrides security.

Gurjivan Singh Sidhu, Nathana: The Punjabi Literature and Arts Centre UK held its annual literary event in Southall. At the opening, Manpreet Singh Baddhani welcomed guests with 'Ji Aayaan' and outlined the program. Azim Sheikh noted that the first session was chaired by Yesh Sathi, Gurcharan Saggu, Mahinderpal Singh Dhillon, Prakash Sohal, and Prof. Shingara Singh Dhaliwal.

The event honored Dr. Sathi Ludhianvi and Chaman Lal Chaman. Santokh Singh Dhillon read excerpts from Dr. Sathiâs debut and final novel, 'Sahil', while scholars offered critical insights. MP Virender Sharma officially launched the book. The segment was moderated by Gurnam Grewal and Manjit Kaur Padda. The Kavi Darbar (poetry session) was led by Iqbal Barar, Davinder Naura, Kulwant Kaur Dhaliwal, Dalbir Kaur, Santokh Singh Dhillon, and Rajinderjeet.

Poets and poetesses including Davinder Naura, Jaswinder Maan, Omkar Manav, Rup Davinder Kaur, Hardeep Basra, Sikander Barar, Dalvir Kaur, Santokh Bhullar, Iqbal Barar, Manpreet Kaur, Mandeep Randhawa, Gurbachan Azaad, Kesi Mohan, Bittoo Khangura, Jasveer Jass, Bhindar Jalalabad, Beant Kaur, Gurcharan Saggu, Jasmer Singh Laal, Neelam Jogan, Sri Ram SarmÄ MÄ«t, Councillor Mahinder Mitta, Balwinder Sharma, Talvinder Dhaliwal, Manmohan Mehru, Dr. Mangat Rai Bhardwaj, Prakash Sohal, and Jagraj Singh Sran â among many others â performed their work. Councillor Kamaljit Kaur Sahota also attended.

But inside the event, chaos erupted â people were terrified. Prof. Shingara Singh Dhaliwal claimed it was a coordinated plot: underworld figures attempted to silence dissenting voices, threatening poets who dared to critique political corruption and royal hypocrisy in their verses. Police later recovered a discarded pistol near the venue â allegedly left by poets as a chilling message. To avoid panic, the organizers buried the story on social media.

article_content:
Liberians vote Tuesday on whether to give football legend George Weah a second term as president, with peace among voters' main concerns in a nation still scarred by back-to-back civil wars. The main political parties have pledged that the presidential and legislative elections in the West African country will pass off peacefully. But the recent killing of three people in clashes between their supporters has fuelled fears of a return to violence. Trouble also marred the close of Weah's re-election campaign Sunday, with his supporters and opposition members throwing stones at each other and police intervening with tear gas. AFP counted at least five men with injuries, some with large gashes on their heads. 'What we expect most is peace â and a strong leader who keeps order,' said Melvine Zoega, 37, among a group of men discussing their concerns in the city of Buchanan, 150 kilometres (90 miles) east of the capital Monrovia. Healthcare, education and roads, jobs and the cost of living all came up, but only after fears of a return to violence. Between 1989 and 2003, the conflicts in Liberia left more than 250,000 people dead. Incumbent Weah, 57, who won the 2017 elections, faces 19 presidential candidates and a likely second-round runoff in early November. But he has campaigned on the slogan 'One round victory'. 'We must all cherish this peace and continue to preserve it, because without peace, our world will be difficult,' Weah told thousands of people gathered in Monrovia Sunday. 'Without peace, development will not take place.' The former international footballer came to power promising to create jobs and invest in education, but critics say he has failed to keep his pledges. The authorities have vowed to track down troublemakers and the national electoral commission is seeking to reassure people it can organise fair and credible polls. 'Everything's ready... We anticipate that all should go well,' said commission chairperson Davidetta Browne-Lansanah. This election is the first held since the United Nations ended its peacekeeping mission in Liberia in 2018. The European Union, the African Union, the West African bloc, ECOWAS, and the United States have deployed observers, in a region hit by a string of recent coups. Polling stations are open from 0800 GMT to 1800 GMT, with the 2.4 million voters also electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate. First results are expected within 15 days. Former vice president Joseph Boakai, who lost to Weah six years ago, is among the frontrunners for the presidency. He has said that any vote cheating or manipulation will lead to 'the end of this country'. The 78-year-old has forged alliances including with former warlord and senator Prince Johnson, who has threatened a popular revolt if the ruling party manipulates the elections. Boakai has pledged to restore the country's image, develop infrastructure and improve life for the poorest. More than a fifth of the population lives on less than $2.15 a day, according to the World Bank, and the price of staple foods has soared. Boakai, who served as vice president between 2006 and 2018, presents himself as an honest alternative to Weah, whom he accuses of presiding over a corrupt system. The United States has sanctioned five senior Liberian officials for alleged corruption in three years. The watchdog Transparency International ranked Liberia 142nd of 180 countries in its 2022 corruption perceptions index. Corruption is not a key concern, however, for George Mobo, in Monrovia's West Point slum. 'Look at African countries and tell me which country is not corrupt,' the 30-year-old said. Education, peace and job creation are his top priorities. His friends agreed, sitting near a brand-new football stadium, built under the president's watch. 'President Weah is the man of the situation. He built roads, made education free, and defeated the coronavirus through strategic leadership. Now he will do better,' said John Seaton, 24. article_content: Off the pace in Serie A, Roma may once again be relying on Jose Mourinho to lead them on a long European run in order to save their season. Mourinho is into his third campaign in charge in the Italian capital and has already led Roma to victory in the inaugural Europa Conference League and then to a Europa League final which they lost on penalties to Sevilla. Yet in Serie A they continue to lag behind, having finished sixth in each of the Portuguese coach's two campaigns so far. They are currently seventh, 11 games into this season, and that is only after a dramatic comeback to beat Lecce 2-1 at the Stadio Olimpico last weekend, with Sardar Azmoun and Romelu Lukaku both scoring stoppage-time goals. Roma are 11 points adrift of the leaders, Mourinho's old side Inter, and four points behind Napoli in fourth, with a derby showdown against Lazio to come this Sunday. It is possible, then, that they may require Europa League success if they are to make it into next season's Champions League, which is the stage where they and Mourinho really want to be. Handed a kind draw, Roma have a 100 percent record so far in Group G, having beaten Sheriff Tiraspol 2-1 in Moldova and Swiss side Servette 4-0 at home before a 2-0 defeat of Slavia Prague last time out. They now travel to the Czech capital to face Slavia again on Thursday, knowing a win will secure their place in the knockout phase again. Lukaku's form has been key for Roma this season, both domestically and in Europe, with the Belgian striker having scored nine times in 12 games since joining on loan from Chelsea at the end of his most recent spell at Inter. He has notably netted in every Europa League game so far and Roma's chances of reaching a third European final in as many seasons under Mourinho may hinge on Lukaku staying fit and firing.
